component_records.title: Project management, governance and weekly reporting
component_records.description: A dedicated project manager and named technical staff are assigned under a written personnel management plan, and the team holds weekly progress, budget and timeline meetings with the City's Accounting and IT leads for the life of the engagement. The plan sets out the task sequence and timeline anchored to the July 1, 2026 go-live, with a milestone schedule for configuration, migration, training and cutover. The project manager maintains a risk and issue log and a change control log so that scope changes are priced before they are accepted. The team also confirms the City's auditing and reporting requirements at mobilisation and records them as design inputs for the account structure and report set.

component_records.title: Hosted accounting and financial reporting platform
component_records.description: The City is provided a cloud-hosted accounting and financial reporting system, procured as a subscription and configured rather than built, with the vendor responsible for hosting, patching and availability. The configured modules are General Ledger, Accounts Payable with 1099 filing, purchasing requisitions and purchase orders routed through approval workflows, Accounts Receivable, Payroll, Utility Billing and Business Licensing, each demonstrated against the City's current Fund Balance processes. The system captures transactions at entry with systematic coding, holds budgeting and forecasting capability including budget-to-actual monitoring, and produces financial reports and data extracts for analysis and decision-making. Every transaction carries an audit trail and retained documentation so records remain auditable for future reference. Licensing is sized for the City's five current users, with named and concurrent licence tiers offered so the City can add users at a published rate.

component_records.title: Account structure design and financial report writing
component_records.description: The implementation lead recommends a chart of accounts and fund structure that supports auditable reporting, mapped from the City's existing Fund Balance structure and aligned to the City's audit and reporting requirements. The team then builds the report library with City staff, writing the financial statements, budget-to-actual reports and management reports the City needs, and hands over report-writing templates so staff can maintain them. Account number customisation is documented in a configuration guide covering segment length, fund, department and object coding, and the rules for adding new codes. The design is signed off by the City's Accounting lead before configuration is frozen.

component_records.title: Data migration of five years of history
component_records.description: The team extracts, cleans and imports the prior five years of accounting history from the City's current Fund Balance system into the new platform, covering general ledger balances and transactions, vendor and customer records, open purchase orders and utility billing account history. Migration runs in three passes: a trial load in a test environment, a reconciliation pass where the City's Accounting staff agree opening balances and historical reports to source, and a final load before cutover. The migration specialist works to a data mapping specification agreed with Accounting and IT, and the cutover plan sequences the freeze of the legacy system, the final load and the validation checks so that disruption and downtime are minimised. A parallel run of at least one full accounting cycle is scheduled before the legacy system is retired.

component_records.title: Training and change management
component_records.description: Power users in Accounting, Utility Billing and Business Licensing receive personalised, role-based training with written manuals for their modules, delivered on site and virtually during implementation. All remaining staff receive at least one recorded training session plus a written manual covering the transactions they will enter, and the recordings are retained by the City for onboarding new staff. Training is offered at each licence level so the City can see what a full user, an approver and a read-only user each receive, and the delivery mode for each course is stated as in-person, virtual or recorded. A short change management plan covers communication to staff and vendors, the cutover weekend, and the support routes available in the first weeks after go-live.

component_records.title: Go-live, post-implementation support and help desk
component_records.description: The platform goes live on July 1, 2026 at the start of the City's fiscal year, with the vendor's team on hand through the first close cycle. Twelve months of post-implementation support begins at go-live and covers the help desk, defect resolution, report adjustments and quarterly check-ins, with response and resolution targets stated by severity. Support is delivered through a ticketing system that logs, prioritises and reports every request so the City can see queue status and ageing. Automated product updates are applied by the vendor on a published release calendar, and each release is accompanied by written communication of the software changes and their effect on the City's configuration. Annual e-filing for 1099s and W-2s is supported each filing season, including the first cycle after go-live. Ongoing support continues through each annual contract renewal under a named account manager.

component_records.title: Third-party components and integration disclosure
component_records.description: The solution is delivered from a single core platform, and any additional application or third-party vendor needed to meet a requirement is identified by name, by the requirement it serves, and by the phase in which it is introduced. Typical candidates are a payroll tax filing service, a check and remittance print service and a bank reconciliation feed, each named in the response with its role and cost. The response states where the City's own IT environment or a third party is relied on, such as network access, single sign-on or the bank interface, so the City can see the boundary of vendor responsibility. Costs and fees for each additional application or vendor are estimated separately in the price proposal.

component_records.title: Price proposal and capped reimbursables
component_records.description: The price proposal is built on Attachment A and references each Section 5 task and deliverable, with the implementation fee and recurring fees broken out in detail by phase, resource and deliverable. Licence fees are broken out separately by module and by licence tier, and support fees are shown with implementation-period support separated from post-implementation and ongoing support. The proposal states a total price for all services and deliverables, a total reimbursable expenses cap, and a total price proposal amount, and the reimbursable cap is a fixed ceiling with no unlimited expense line. Costs and fees for any additional application or vendor are estimated as a separate line. The price is submitted as final and is not revised during clarification.

component_records.title: Contract, compliance and communication obligations
component_records.description: A contract and compliance workstream owns the non-technical obligations. It obtains and reviews the City's standard contract for services and the General Contract Terms and Conditions before submission and confirms the proposal is submitted on the City's terms with no additional or modified terms attached, accepting that the City may decline any modification requested. It runs a single point of contact discipline so that no team member, subcontractor or supplier communicates about the proposal outside the City's permitted channels from submission to award. It prepares Attachment G documentation of the financial data protection measures and secure access controls, including encryption, role-based access, multi-factor authentication and audit logging. It provides the Certificate of Insurance for workers compensation and commercial general liability, and the Certification of Financial Condition signed by an authorised officer, with a diary to notify the City of any material change to that certification within thirty days and to notify the Contract Lead within fifteen days. It files the location-of-workers disclosure covering where work is performed and any use of resources outside the United States, and gives written notice of any relocation of personnel outside the United States. It carries the cost of proposal preparation and interview attendance as a bid cost with no claim on the City, and it staffs the virtual finalists' interview on September 25, 2025 if the City calls one.

component_records.title: Implementation experience and references
component_records.description: The response evidences at least three comparable implementations for local government, regional councils of government or federal grant-funded organisations, each with the client name, scope, performance dates and a contact with a valid email address. Each case study states the key staff who worked on it and how the results were measured, such as close-cycle time, audit findings cleared or manual steps removed. The team also evidences advisory work streamlining client procedures and continued support for improvements and daily operations, drawn from the same reference base. A local referral is offered for an in-person demonstration where one is available.

Neither document is in the RFP; they are available only on request. The bidder therefore prices and accepts an unseen contract, and any term it cannot live with (indemnity, liability cap, termination, payment timing) cannot be raised after submission. The documents are absent from the RFP and the City will not evaluate modified terms, so the bidder commits to unknown obligations at a fixed price with no route to negotiate afterwards.
items.reason: Review requirement, enforceable terms, rejection of modified terms, availability on request all stated in sources.

items.text: July 1, 2026 go-live treated as firm against an award date the RFP does not fix. The proposed solution builds the plan backwards from a firm July 1, 2026 go-live and assumes contract award in late October 2025, but the RFP describes July 1, 2026 only as a goal and gives no award or start date. If award slips, or if the City later treats the date as contractual, the bidder absorbs a compressed mobilisation, configuration, five-year migration, training and parallel run, or misses a date that gates acceptance. The schedule risk is real because the RFP leaves both the award date and the binding nature of the go-live date open, while the solution has already committed to the date as firm.
items.reason: Go-live goal and no award-to-start date supported; late October award assumption, five-year migration, parallel run, acceptance gating not in cited sources.

items.text: Five-year data migration scoped without knowing source volumes or formats. The solution commits to extracting, cleaning and importing five years of general ledger, vendor, customer, open purchase order and utility billing history from Fund Balance, with three load passes and a parallel accounting cycle. The RFP does not state data volumes, file formats or whether Tyler will cooperate with extraction. Underestimated volume or a hostile extract turns a fixed-fee migration into unbudgeted rework and threatens the go-live. Migration is a fixed-fee commitment in the solution while the RFP leaves volumes, formats and third-party cooperation unstated, so the effort could be several times the estimate.
items.reason: Five-year import and Tyler Fund Balance supported; three load passes, parallel cycle, fixed-fee, specific data types, unstated volumes not shown.

items.text: Hard copy original and emailed copy both due at the same 4:00 PM deadline. The RFP requires one signed original proposal in hard copy and a digital copy emailed to accounting@colfax-ca.gov, with late proposals not considered, but does not say whether the 4:00 PM PST deadline on August 28, 2025 governs physical receipt in Colfax. A courier delay or a missing signature on the original makes an otherwise compliant proposal unevaluable. Rejection is total and the RFP leaves the hard-copy receipt rule unclear, so a single logistics failure ends the bid.
items.reason: Hard copy, email, late rejection supported; however the source states the hard copy must be received by the deadline, so 'unclear' is contradicted.

items.text: Attachment E and Attachment G referenced but not supplied. The RFP points to Attachment E for the Certificate of Insurance and key personnel experience and to Attachment G for the financial data protection and secure access documentation, but neither is in the document set. The solution prepares a written Attachment G narrative and control matrix against a recognised framework on the assumption the City has set no standard, and offers insurance at customary municipal limits. If the City expects a prescribed form or specific control framework, both submissions need rework close to the deadline. Both attachments are missing and the solution fills the gap with assumptions, so rework is likely unless the City confirms the expected format.
items.reason: Attachment E is a Certificate of Insurance only, not key personnel experience; Attachment E and G text actually appear in sources, so 'not supplied' is overstated.

items.text: Conflicting certification notice periods create a compliance trap. R107 requires notice to the City within thirty days of anything that materially alters the financial condition certification, while R146 requires notice to the Contract Lead within fifteen days. The solution applies the shorter period and copies the City, which is workable only if the Contract Lead is identified and reachable; the RFP does not name the Contract Lead or the delivery method. The conflict is certain but the practical impact is a compliance breach rather than project failure, and the solution already mitigates it by applying the shorter period.
items.reason: 30-day and 15-day notice periods conflict as stated; Contract Lead is not named in sources.

items.text: Module scope and user count left open while the price is fixed. The RFP lists six Fund Balance modules and five current users but does not say whether all six must be replicated or whether five is the licensed count to price. The solution assumes all six modules are in scope and prices five users with additional users at a published rate. If the City expects more users or a module the solution treats as optional, the fixed price is understated and the licence line is wrong. The RFP leaves both the module scope and the licensing basis unsettled, and the solution resolves them by assumption in a price that cannot be revised.
items.reason: Six modules and five users listed; sources do not state the licensed count; assumptions and price revisability are bidder positions.

items.text: Reimbursable expenses cap set by the bidder with no City guidance. The RFP requires a capped reimbursable expenses figure and a total cap line but gives no ceiling or method, and the solution sets its own fixed dollar ceiling covering travel and third-party filing fees. If travel to the Sierra foothills site, on-site training and 1099/W-2 filing fees exceed the cap, the bidder absorbs the difference; if the cap is set high, the total price looks uncompetitive against a 20% fee weighting. The cap is a bidder choice against an unstated City expectation, so the exposure is a margin or a scoring loss rather than project failure.
items.reason: Cap requirement and total cap line supported; 20% fee weighting, Sierra foothills travel, and 1099/W-2 filing fees not in cited sources.

items.text: Third-party components and offshore resourcing disclosed without knowing the City's tolerance. The solution names payroll tax filing, check and remittance print and bank reconciliation feed as likely third-party components and must disclose where work is performed and any resources outside the United States. The RFP does not say whether third-party applications are permitted or how the City weighs offshore delivery, and it says the City will evaluate the associated risks and costs before award. A City that dislikes either can mark the proposal down or reject it. The RFP leaves permission and evaluation criteria open while the solution depends on named third parties, so the outcome turns on facts the RFP does not settle.
items.reason: Offshore disclosure and City risk/cost evaluation are supported; the named payroll tax, check print, and bank feed components are not in the sources.

items.text: Twenty-page limit against a 45% scope criterion and five attachments. The proposal must cover goals and scope, technical support, fee proposal and schedule, qualifications and references, plus Attachments A to G, within 20 pages plus two for the cover letter and five for appendices, and the RFP does not say whether over-length is rejected or penalised. The solution's component set is broad, so the bid team risks either an over-length proposal or thin answers on the highest-weighted criterion. The page limit is stated as a should while surrounding format rules are mandatory, so the consequence of over-length is genuinely unclear and the content pressure is real.
items.reason: Page limits and weights are supported; 'Attachments A to G' is unsupported (only A–D cited), and 'should' wording is only partly shown.

items.text: Prohibited-communications rule reaches subcontractors and suppliers. From submission to award, no team member, subcontractor or supplier may communicate about the proposal outside permitted channels, and the City's harmless-and-unintentional waiver has no stated criteria. The solution relies on named third-party vendors for payroll tax filing, check print and bank feeds, and any routine vendor contact with City staff during the evaluation window could disqualify the proposal. Disqualification would be severe, but the solution already runs a single point of contact discipline, so a breach needs an unusual lapse by a third party.
items.reason: Communication rule and subcontractor reach supported; named vendors and single point of contact discipline are not in sources, and waiver criteria are only implied.
